claims.text: The untreated as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Sharp internal lamellar or colony boundaries promote dislocation pile-ups.
Dislocation pile-ups at the internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and premature tensile failure.
The proposed intervention is annealing at approximately 700°C for approximately 30 minutes under argon, followed by quenching to room temperature.
Short, moderate-temperature annealing will promote limited atomic interdiffusion at the dual-phase lamellar or colony boundaries.
The annealing-induced interfacial modification may constitute a complexion transition.
Interfacial diffusion will smooth compositional gradients and structural mismatches at the phase boundaries.
The modified interfaces will be less effective barriers to dislocation motion.
The modified interfaces will facilitate dislocation transmission across colony boundaries.
Easier dislocation transmission will reduce dislocation pile-ups and associated local stress concentrations.
Reduced interfacial stress concentrations will delay microcrack initiation during tensile deformation.
The fine eutectic microstructure will continue to provide strength after the controlled annealing treatment.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the annealed alloy will exhibit significantly improved room-temperature tensile ductility.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the annealed alloy will retain or possibly increase its strength.
Insufficient annealing temperature or duration may fail to modify the interfaces adequately.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration may cause grain coarsening or phase decomposition.
Annealing-induced grain coarsening or phase decomposition would reduce strength.
The proposed performance comparison applies to room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing at a strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
